acts.title: Text A · What people say they do
text: A survey published last year asked two thousand viewers about their habits, and the results were unusually contradictory.

Ninety-one per cent said that they regularly binge-watched. Asked how many episodes they watched at a sitting, most reported three. When they were asked whether they enjoyed it, almost everybody said they did.

The interviewer then asked the same people whether binge-watching was a good thing. The majority said it was not. Several told the researchers that they felt slightly ashamed afterwards, and one said she had cancelled a subscription twice and resubscribed twice.

The report’s authors pointed out that nobody had asked the viewers to justify the contradiction, and that they had not offered to. People know perfectly well what they are doing. They simply do it anyway.

items.q: What did the survey find?
o: People binge-watch, enjoy it, and disapprove of it at the same time

items.q: What did the report’s authors point out?
o: Nobody had asked the viewers to explain the contradiction

acts.title: Text B · What changed, and when
text: Until about 2007, a series arrived one episode a week, and the industry assumed that was a limitation rather than a design.

When the first services released a whole season at once, executives were asked whether audiences would pace themselves. They said they expected people to watch roughly one a week. They were wrong by a factor of about four.

What that changed was the writing. A weekly episode had to remind you what had happened; a binged one does not. Writers told interviewers that they had stopped writing recaps within two years, and that the plots had become considerably more complex as a result.
One showrunner said the shift had cost the industry something too. Nobody, she said, now spends a week arguing about what will happen next — and that argument used to be free advertising.

items.s: Before 2007 a weekly release was seen as a limitation.
Executives correctly predicted how fast audiences would watch.
Writers stopped including recaps within about two years.
Plots became simpler as a result.
One showrunner thought the industry had lost something.

acts.title: Reporting what was said and asked
rule: When you report speech, three things move: the tense steps back, the pronouns change to fit the new speaker, and — in a question — the word order returns to that of a statement. The third of these is the one that separates B1 from B2, because it is the one that survives into writing.
points: present → past, past → past perfect, present perfect → past perfect, will → would, can → could.
A past perfect is already as far back as it goes. So are should have, could have and would.
If the statement is still true, the present is often kept: She said the office is on the third floor.
No auxiliary, no inversion, no question mark. He asked where I worked.
Joined with whether or if: She asked whether I had enjoyed it.
tell me, tell him. say does not take one directly: say to me.
eg: “We binge-watch.” → They said they binge-watched.
Present to past.
“I cancelled it twice.” → She said she had cancelled it twice.
Past to past perfect.
“We have stopped.” → They said they had stopped.
Present perfect to past perfect.
“It will change.” → He said it would change.
will to would.
“I can’t explain it.” → She said she couldn’t explain it.
can to could.
“Where do you work?” → He asked where I worked.
Statement order, no did.
“Did you enjoy it?” → She asked whether I had enjoyed it.
whether, and no question mark.
“Don’t be late.” → He told me not to be late.
tell + object + to + infinitive.
She told me the meeting was cancelled.
tell takes a person directly.
She said to me that the meeting was cancelled.
say needs to before the person.
acts.careful: “He asked where did I work” and “She said me it was cancelled” are the two errors that appear in almost every B2 script. A reported question is not a question, and say never takes a person without to.

acts.title: Direct into reported, in four moves
steps: She said: “I cancelled my subscription last year.”
1 · Change the PRONOUN: I becomes she.
She said that she had cancelled …
2 · Step the TENSE back: cancelled becomes had cancelled.
She said that she had cancelled her subscription …
3 · Change any possessive: my becomes her.
She said that she had cancelled her subscription the previous year.
4 · Change the TIME WORD: last year becomes the previous year.

write.q: Ask three people you know how they watch television, and report what they said in about 180 words. Report at least four statements and at least two questions. Every reported question must use statement word order and end with a full stop.
write.model:
I asked three people how they actually watch things, and got three different answers.

My sister said she almost never watched anything alone. She told me she had stopped subscribing to two services because nobody in the house could agree, and that they now watched one episode a night, together, like 1994.

A colleague said the opposite. He told me he had watched an entire eight-part series on a Saturday and had felt terrible afterwards, and he asked whether that counted as a hobby. I said I did not know.

The third was my father, who asked why I wanted to know and then answered anyway. He said he watched the news at nine and nothing else, and that he could not understand what the rest of us were doing with our evenings.

What surprised me was that all three of them apologized for their answer. I had not asked anybody to justify anything, and every one of them did.
